messages.subject: spatial models
messages.body_plain:
Rather than assuming that all of my sites are completely (and
identically) "independent", I'm wondering if it would be possible to
incorporate the Euclidian distances between each pair into the
analysis.  So then the assumption would be that the "independence" of
any two sites is a linear function of the distance between them.  I
don't know much about this (obviously), but my impression is that this
is how phylogenetic comparative methods work -the
independence of two species is a function of the phylogenetic distance
between them.

Would it be possible to do this in a pcount or occu
 model by doing something like fixing the covariance matrix to be a matrix
of the geographic distances between each pair of sites?

I saw a few threads related to assessing spatial dependence of model residuals post-hoc, but couldn't find anything about incorporating spatial effects explicitly into the models.  But I apologize if I've missed earlier discussions of this!

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] spatial models
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

you can find code in the literature on how to fit CAR spatial random effects into occupancy or Nmix models using WinBUGS and OpenBUGS. There are also a couple of R packages that allow you to fit static occupancy models with CAR or related spatial processes:
- stocc: CAR and so-called restricted spatial regression; does static occupancy using Bayesian MCMC
- hSDM: does CAR for static occupancy using MCMC (but does not call the model an occupancy model; one of them is exactly a static occupancy model)
- Paul Conn has written an R package to do hierarchical distance sampling with CAR priors, I believe. Can't remember the name now.

Plus, there must be a couple of others. The trouble is that most spatial statisticians don't go into the field ever and so are not aware of the benefits of adding a model component for imperfect detection (i.e., there will be lots of packages that allow you to fit spatial models to relative occurrence and relative abundance).

Kind regards  --  Marc

Dear colleagues,

I have snow track counts from 319 transects (2 temporal reps; 5 sites with both visits missing) and want to analyse them using the Royle-Nichols model (after reduction to detection/nondetection). However, occuRN crashes for some dimension match problem:

>    summary(fm1 <- occuRN(~1 ~ 1, data=umf))    # Null RN model
Warnmeldungen:
1: 5 sites have been discarded because of missing data.
2: In matrix(plogis(V %*% parms[(nOP + 1):nP] + V.offset), M, J, byrow = TRUE) :
  Datenlänge [628] ist kein Teiler oder Vielfaches der Anzahl der Zeilen [319]
Fehler in summary(fm1 <- occuRN(~1 ~ 1, data = umf)) :
  Fehler bei der Auswertung des Argumentes 'object' bei der Methodenauswahl
für Funktion 'summary': Fehler in cp.in <http://cp.in> * lambda.in <http://lambda.in> : nicht passende Arrays

In contrast, the simple occupancy model runs fine:

>  occu(~1 ~ 1, data=umf)    # Null RN model

Call:
occu(formula = ~1 ~ 1, data = umf)

Occupancy:
 Estimate    SE    z  P(>|z|)
     1.79 0.206 8.68 3.98e-18
[....]

Btw, the Nmix model (function pcount()) works fine for the counts version of the data, with the fives sites with NAs included:
>    summary(fm1 <- pcount(~1 ~ 1, data=umfcounts))    # Null Nmix model

Call:
pcount(formula = ~1 ~ 1, data = umfcounts)

Abundance (log-scale):
 Estimate     SE    z  P(>|z|)
     1.02 0.0766 13.3 1.45e-40
[....]

Any ideas what could be wrong would be appreciated.

Thanks and kind regards  --  Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] mapping spatial predictions using pcount
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hannah,

As you suspected, you need to include the offset in the linear model.
However, I don't think it is ideal to use transect length as an offset
of abundance. Can you use the area sampled instead? If the transects
had fixed widths, and were narrow enough to make distance-related
heterogeneity in detection negligible, then you could use (log)
transect area as an offset to estimate density. Then you could scale
that up to the level of a raster pixel.

Richard

Hmmmm.

How about the rest of my equation attempting to replicate manually what Predict does with pcount, does that look correct at least?
Hannah

messages.body_plain:
Hi Hannah,

Maybe Marc and Andy can weigh in on what they think is the best
option. I know that in the past they have used transect length in some
way as an offset of the number of individuals exposed to sampling.
That might be a good option, but I don't think they simply used
offset(log(length)). One paper that proposes a nice modeling framework
for this type of data is Royle et al (2011, MEE):

http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.2041-210X.2011.00116.x/full

but the model requires that the individuals (snares in your case) are
marked. Perhaps it's something to consider if you continue sampling.

Richard

This is why it is better, in my opinion, to model density rather
abundance in some unknown area. Since you don't have either fixed area
plots or distance data, you can't really get at density, but you
should be able to map the expected number of snares exposed to
sampling, given some transect length and the pixel-level covariates.
But note that this is different than the expected number of snares in
some pixel of your raster.

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Hello unmarked users,
  I recently ran the goodness of fit code provided in the help file for parboot and the results were not encouraging:

I wonder if anyone has thoughts to share on what might be causing my problem(s) and perhaps provide a solution that is better than the one I am currently applying to the situation (alcohol).

Thanks,

Andrew Cox
Dept of Biology
University of Nebraska - Omaha
